sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: We introduce the Extender, a log-structured variant of the standard Transformer architecture. In a standard Transformer, each layer communicates with subsequent layers exclusively via the residual $\mathbf{h}$, a superposition channel. The Extender adds a concatenation channel $\mathbf{x}$: each layer $\ell$ emits both a residual update $δ_\ell$ which is added to $\mathbf{h}$, and a much smaller extension $ε_\ell$ which is appended to $\mathbf{x}$. While both the FFN and $\mathbf{q}$ see $\mathbf{h}$, the attention $\mathbf{kv}$ projections take only $\mathbf{x}$ as input. As a result, the fully extended $\mathbf{x}$ contains the complete input for the $\mathbf{kv}$ projections of all layers, reducing the persistent attention memory footprint from $2Ld_{model}$ to $\sum|ε_\ell|$. We find that with $|ε_\ell|=32$, the Extender matches Transformer accuracy on short-context (CORE) tasks at 199M-924M parameters, and exceeds Transformer accuracy on long-context (RULER) workloads, again at 924M parameters. For our 1664-wide, 924M model, the Extender's persistent attention memory footprint is $104\times$ smaller than MHA. The memory savings grow with model width.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: The residual stream is fundamental to the standard Transformer model: it is the sole input to every layer; the sole output of each layer is an update to the residual stream. Arguably, its most important function is that of mitigating vanishing gradients in deep models: each individual layer sees direct gradient from the final loss computation, enabling stable optimization. In other words, the loss directly teaches each layer how to predict the next token. However, this design is not without drawbacks. While each layer may in practice only make small changes, the residual update from each layer is full width, making each feature of the input to the subsequent attention layer unique. During inference, this requires each attention layer to maintain its own, full-width residual (h) or key-value (kv) cache to avoid very costly recomputation. The memory footprint of these caches grows linearly with model width 𝑑𝑚𝑜𝑑𝑒𝑙, depth 𝐿 and context length 𝑇. For large language model, the aggregate kv-cache alone can exceed 100 GB before dimensionality reduction, layer reuse, quantization and other space-saving optimizations. Moreover, beyond predicting the next token, each layer ℓ may also need to communicate its own findings, say 𝜙ℓ to subsequent layers. Here, 𝜙ℓ may not look anything like the next token; for example, it may encode distance from another token, or repetition counter, yet this too must be communicated through the residual, potentially in contention with other writes, and against the teachings of the loss. The Extender is log-structured variation on the classic Transformer architecture that separates the next-token prediction stream from the attention input. Similar to the Transformer, the Extender is made up of stack of Extender layers, each consisting of several individual sub-layers, but dominated by softmax attention and FFN. However, instead of giving the attention sub-layers full visibility into the output of the previous layer, the Extender provides two distinct channels: The conventional residual, used primarily for predicting the next token. Each layer contributes full-width residual update 𝛿ℓ, such that hℓ = hℓ 1 + 𝑤ℓ 𝛿ℓ, where 𝑤ℓ is scalar weight. hℓ is part of the input to the FFN sub-layer of the next block, as well as to attention (q only, not kv), and the final logit projection. h1 = [𝑒𝑚𝑏𝑒𝑑 (𝑡)]. 1 Each layer ℓ contributes information to subsequent attention kv and projections via small, readonly feature extension 𝜖ℓ to log-structured token embedding. The extended embedding after layer ℓ is xℓ = [xℓ 1; 𝑅𝑀𝑆𝑁𝑜𝑟𝑚(𝜖ℓ)] where x-1 = [𝑒𝑚𝑏𝑒𝑑 (𝑡)]. We use to refer to the fully extended embedding after the token has traversed all 𝐿 layers. As the in the notation implies, the append-only nature of in the Extender architecture means that contains every 𝑥ℓ, ℓ [0..𝐿-1] as prefix. Therefore, while every layer sees different xℓ, single shared x-cache suffices across all attention sub-layers. Thus while the Multi-Head Attention (MHA) Vaswani et al. (2017) Transformer requires kv-cache memory proportional to 2𝑇 𝐿𝑑model (two 𝑑𝑚𝑜𝑑𝑒𝑙-wide vectors per layer, per token), the Extender instead requires x-cache memory 𝑇 𝐿𝑑 𝜖 (one 𝑑 𝜖 -wide extension per layer, per token), reducing the persistent attention memory footprint at long context lengths by up to 2𝑑𝑚𝑜𝑑𝑒𝑙 vs. MHA. The model sizes we tested, 198M/436M/920M, with 𝑑 𝜖 =32, the Extender matches our Reference Transformer on short-context tasks ( +1 on CORE), and leads significantly on long-context (RULER) tasks. 𝑑𝜖 To compute softmax attention without kv-cache, x-cache based attention would have to repeatedly re-materialize kv from x, potentially resulting in significant computational overhead. To resolve this, the Extender features an ephemeral kv-cache at inference time. The ephemeral kv-cache of given layer may be materialized on-demand from the x-cache by multiplication with the relevant attention 𝑊𝑘 and 𝑊𝑣 matrices. Amortized over multiple input and output tokens, this kv materialization cost is small. Thus the ephemeral kv-cache may be released between turns, as needed. Because of the large attention memory footprint of MHA, it is rarely used in its pure form in large models. Instead, models that retain softmax attention use techniques such as dimensionality reduction Shazeer (2019); Ainslie et al. (2023); DeepSeek-AI (2024), layer reuse Liu et al. (2024a); Sun et al. (2024); Wu & Tu (2024); Brandon et al. (2024); Zuhri et al. (2024) and quantization Xiao et al. (2023); Frantar et al. (2023); Liu et al. (2024b) to limit the footprint. The Extender instead changes the architecture, separating the per-layer next-token prediction 𝛿ℓ from the per-token features 𝜖ℓ that persist in attention memory. The result is compact attention memory footprint between turns, while achieving similar accuracy on short-context and better accuracy on long-context tasks. During turns, memory requirements are unchanged vs standard Transformer. However, existing dimensionality reduction, layer reuse and quantization methods may still be applied to attention during turns, if desired. Our experiments with GQA (See Appendix D) suggest that Grouped Query Attention combines well with the Extender. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. 2 briefly introduces past work on reducing attention memory footprint. 3 presents the Extender in more detail, and 4 discusses inference considerations. 5 compares Extender accuracy vs. Reference Transformer on short-context (DCLM CORE) and long-context (RULER) tasks, and 6 concludes. Additional results and analysis, including GQA, knowledge distillation and scaling results are available in the Appendix.

sections.title: 2 Background
sections.content: Because the attention memory footprint of standard softmax multi-head attention Transformer grows linearly with model width 𝑑𝑚𝑜𝑑𝑒𝑙, layer depth 𝐿 and context length 𝑇, variety of memoryreduction approaches have been proposed. The Extender reduces persistent attention memory: the memory required between turns, while remaining compatible with existing approaches during turn. That said, because method that applies during turn applies equally between turns, we briefly review the related work below. Dimensionality Reduction With grouped query attention (GQA) Ainslie et al. (2023), an attention layer with 𝐻 query heads may maintain only 𝐻/4 or 𝐻/8 keys and values per token. This in turn reduces attention memory requirements by 48, at modest accuracy loss vs. full MHA. Multihead Latent Attention (MLA) DeepSeek-AI (2024) instead stores compressed version of the kv pair, as much as 10 smaller. This is decompressed on-demand before attention. As result, MLA does not need to reduce the number of kv heads, but may suffer compression losses instead. The Extender instead changes what the attention layer reads. However, GQA can be applied to the Extender to reduce memory footprint during turns (see Appendix D). 2 Layer Reuse YOCO and LCKV move toward one shared cache Sun et al. (2024); Wu & Tu (2024): YOCO reuses single global KV cache in its cross-decoder. LCKV has most layers use the same first layer KV cache. Cross-Layer Attention (CLA) and MLKV instead share one cache among group of layers Brandon et al. (2024); Zuhri et al. (2024). MiniCache instead merges similar layers KV states after training Liu et al. (2024a). The Extender significantly reuses attention input data, but does not change the attention mechanism. If desired, CLA may be applied to the Extender to save attention memory during turns. We do not evaluate this here. Quantization With quantization Xiao et al. (2023); Frantar et al. (2023); Liu et al. (2024b), individual features or weights are represented using fewer bits, leading to both reduced memory footprint and often improved computational throughput. Applied judiciously, the accuracy loss from quantization can be modest, and savings on the order of 24 are not uncommon. We do not evaluate quantization in this paper.

sections.title: 3.1 Choosing 𝑑 𝜖 and Designing the kv Windows
sections.content: In this paper, we use s=𝑑𝑚𝑜𝑑𝑒𝑙. This makes the Extender attention layer shape identical to that of the Transformer, making direct comparison easier. Given this constraint, we must choose 𝑑 𝜖 , or more generally 𝜖ℓ . Here, we decompose that into setting 𝑑 𝜖 and ℓ𝑚𝑎𝑥, where ℓ𝑚𝑎𝑥 is the final layer that emits an 𝜖. By default, ℓ𝑚𝑎𝑥=𝐿2. Moreover, since for ℓ > 0, xℓ 𝑑𝑚𝑜𝑑𝑒𝑙 each layer ℓ > 0 can only read subset of xℓ. These two design decisions are closely tied: with small 𝑑 𝜖 , it becomes more important that all the features of 𝜖 are seen by subsequent layers. Similarly, with large 𝑑 𝜖 , late layer writes may crowd out the initial embedding and early layer writes, making late layers unable to see critical features. For 4 height =64). With 𝑑 𝜖 =32, (cid:205) 𝜖ℓ =800 features, leaving example our 26-layer model has 𝑑𝑚𝑜𝑑𝑒𝑙=1664 ( width room for 864 input embedding features in s25. with 𝑑 𝜖 =64, (cid:205) 𝜖ℓ =1600 features. Empirically, sizes larger than 64 and smaller than 32 perform significantly worse, and are not evaluated here. With 𝑑 𝜖 =64, the choice of read window is particularly important. Here, sliding window leaves the final layer with only 64 features of the original embedding. Three choices we considered were 𝐹𝑖𝑟 𝑠𝑡, 𝐿𝑎𝑠𝑡, and 𝑅𝑎𝑛𝑑𝑜𝑚, for both the and the projection. For k, we found that 𝐿𝑎𝑠𝑡 is always the better choice. For however, the choice is less obvious: many important tasks involve an identity mapping. Thus must be able to recall enough of the input embedding to produce the correct logit. For these, 𝐿𝑎𝑠𝑡 would be poor choice when 𝑑 𝜖 =64 For many other tasks, 𝐹𝑖𝑟 𝑠𝑡 would instead be poor choice. For 𝑑 𝜖 =64 and ℓ𝑚𝑎𝑥=𝐿2, k=𝐿𝑎𝑠𝑡, v=𝑅𝑎𝑛𝑑𝑜𝑚 may be the better compromise. Another possibility is changing ℓ𝑚𝑎𝑥, preventing later layers from writing to x. For example, setting ℓ𝑚𝑎𝑥=𝐿/2 cuts (cid:205) 𝜖ℓ by half, leaving room for the embedding. We evaluate few of these choices in Appendix B. Our default model uses 𝑑 𝜖 =32, ℓ𝑚𝑎𝑥=𝐿 2, except 𝜖0=64. 4 Inference and the x-Cache By replacing the kv-cache with an x-cache and computing kv from during attention, the Extender could achieve the memory savings claimed above both during and between turns. However, this would incur the compute cost of repeatedly reprojecting kv from x. To address this, the Extender uses an ephemeral kv-cache, which may be freed between turns as desired. This effectively amortizes the cost of reprojecting the kv-cache from the x-cache. It is also worth noting that because the reprojection cost grows linearly with the total kv dimension, using GQA for attention dimensionality reduction kv-cache speeds up the reprojection time by factor similar to the GQA space savings.

sections.title: 5 Evaluation
sections.content: Below, we present results from Extender and Transformer language models trained on the ClimbMix Diao et al. (2025) and ProLong Gao et al. (2025) datasets, using the short-context DCLM CORE Li et al. (2024) and long-context RULER Hsieh et al. (2024) benchmark suites. Reference Transformer In order to better understand the strengths and weaknesses of the Extender, we compare it to Reference Transformer. The Reference Transformer is Llama-style MHA transformer with two small changes, following Andrej Karpathys nanochat Karpathy (2025) design: the Muon optimizer Jordan et al. (2024) instead of AdamW for the large matrices, and SoftCap Gemma Team (2024) in the attention layer (included with Flash Attention-2 Dao (2024)). The Reference Transformer is decoder-only Llama-style Transformer with standard pre-norm residual stream. Token embeddings of dimension 𝑑𝑚𝑜𝑑𝑒𝑙 are processed by 𝐿 identical blocks, each of the form + Attn(RMSNorm(h)), + FFN(RMSNorm(h)), followed by final RMSNorm before unembedding. RMSNorm uses 𝜀=105 and learnable scale. The Extender mirrors the Reference Transformer as closely as possible in terms of shape, activation functions, optimizer, training schedule, weights, norms etc. Below are several common characteristics. By default, we use common multi-head causal attention, with Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE, default 𝜃=106) applied to queries and keys, using the standard half-dimension split. GQA is addressed briefly in Appendix Attention logits are soft-capped as 𝑠 tanh(𝑧/𝑠) with default 𝑠 = 50, using FlashAttention-2 kernel. The feed-forward network is SwiGLU Shazeer (2020), FFN(ℎ) = 𝑊2 (cid:0)SiLU(𝑊1h) 𝑊3h(cid:1), with hidden width 8𝑑/3 rounded up to multiple of 32, and all linear layers bias-free. The default tokenizer is nanochats byte-level BPE, vocabulary 32k. Documents are prefixed with beginning-of-sequence token, and we use document masking for best-fit packed training sequences. 5 Input embeddings and the output projection share single weight matrix (tied embeddings). Parameters are initialized as: embedding rows (0, 1/ 𝑑); multi-dimensional weights Uniform(1/ fan_in); RMSNorm scales are initialized to 1. fan_in, 1/ Models are trained using WSD training schedule Hägele et al. (2024). We use the Muon optimizer Jordan et al. (2024) for the large weight matrices, and the AdamW optimizer Loshchilov & Hutter (2019) for the embedding weights and other one-dimensional tensors, such as norms. Effective batch for ClimbMix 2k was 256 sequences, scaled peak learning rates were: Muon 2.1 102, AdamW 1.41 102 on embeddings, and 8.5 104 on other 1-D parameters. For ProLong 64k, effective batch was 4 sequences, scaled peak LR: Muon 8.8 104 and AdamW 3.5 105 on both AdamW groups. For efficiency, GEMMs run in bfloat16; RoPE Su et al. (2024) frequencies and RMSNorm Zhang & Sennrich (2019) statistics stay in fp32. The design intentionally omits QK-norm, value embeddings, attention residuals, and output logit softcap, all of which could be adapted to the Extender, but would not help characterize the difference between the two architectures. The model parameter counts vary slightly between our Extender and Reference Transformer models due to architecture differences, but model width 𝑑𝑚𝑜𝑑𝑒𝑙 and depth 𝐿 are identical, and as follows. Weve made an effort to use the actual sizes in the tables, plots and analysis, but will use the size class name when discussing multiple models of the same size class but different exact sizes. Size Width Depth Q/K/V Head 𝐿 𝑑𝑚𝑜𝑑𝑒𝑙 dim class 128 13 198M 1024 128 20 436M 1280 128 26 920M 1664 heads 8 10 13 Table 2: Model shape for each size class. The 436M and 920M models have width-to-depth ratio of 64. The 198M model departs slightly from this ratio, to retain 128-feature heads. The size classes are named after the Transformer size. The Extender versions have approximately 0.5% more parameters. We apply an auxiliary regularization cost to each token to prevent runaway residual writes: (cid:205)ℓ relu(RMS(𝛿ℓ) 𝜏)2 with 𝜏=8 and coefficient 3103. After this, later layers still receive 1 𝐿 more weight (𝑤ℓ is often 10 that of the earliest layers), but features of 𝛿ℓ are in healthy range.

sections.title: 5.1 Short Context: DCLM CORE Benchmark suite
sections.content: We trained one Extender and one Reference Transformer of each size class, from scratch, using Chinchilla Hoffmann et al. (2022) token budgets of 20 tokens per model parameter, or approximately 4B, 9B and 18B tokens for the 198M, 436M and 920M parameter models respectively. No finetuning or other task-specific training was applied. Figure 2 shows the performance of these models on the DCLM CORE v1 Li et al. (2024) benchmark suite, using the nanochat Karpathy (2025) CORE harness. We group the 22 CORE benchmarks into categories T-Mono/other. Here, T-Mono is the subset of tasks on which the Transformer score improved monotonically with parameter count under Chinchilla-matched training. Intuitively, monotonic improvement with size suggests more reliable benchmark in this size range. For reference, we also include Llama-3.2-1B scores. This model was pretrained on up to 9 trillion tokens Meta (2024), explaining the large performance gap on some tasks. On other tasks, such as arc_easy, Llamas 500 more training does not improve performance, suggesting the 1B model size is the primary limitation rather than the training or the architecture. Overall, we find that the Extender and Transformer models perform similarly on DCLM CORE tasks, given parameter counts within 1% of each other, and equal training budgets.

Models were not fine-tuned for instruction-following or RULER. As result, these absolute scores are lower than overtrained or fine-tuned public models. Here, we focus on the 920M parameter models, and evaluate them at the pretrain stage, after 2.5B tokens of 64k ProLong data Gao et al. (2025), and after 5B tokens of 64k ProLong respectively, using the recommended 60/40 mix of long vs. short context documents. For 2.5B ProLong training, we kept 𝜃 = 106, and resumed training from the pre-decay pretrain checkpoint, then trained with ProLong tokens finished by brief decay. For 5B ProLong training, we similarly resumed training from the pre-decay checkpoint of the 2.5B training run. The resulting aggregate token count for the 5B ProLong models is 21.3B tokens (some ClimbMix tokens lost here due to pre-decay resume). Figure 3 shows how the Extender and the Reference Transformer performed on RULER for context lengths between 1k and 32k tokens. Results are based on 𝑛=30 samples per task, with greedy decoding. On average, we find that the Extender outperforms the Reference Transformer on these long-context tasks. Two interesting details stand out: the Extender has large advantage on the harder multi-key tasks, while the Transformer wins convincingly at the variable tracking task. This suggests possible difference in inductive bias on these three tasks. However, we did not investigate this further. We define subset NIAH-6 as the six easier tasks: single-key needle-in-a-haystack variants 13 (S1S3), multivalue (MV), multiquery (MQ), and multikey variant 1 (MK1). We use the label REST to refer to the remaining group of tasks (MK23, VT, CWE, FWE, QA1 and QA2). Table 3 reports NIAH-6, REST, and the 13-task RULER mean at each evaluation length, plus T-mono and centered CORE (%) for the ClimbMix 2k base and the 64k ProLong mid-train stages. After the ClimbMix pretrain, and before ProLong training, the Extender is significantly better than the Transformer at context lengths beyond the 2k training context. For 1-2k contexts, any differences are marginal. After ProLong training, the Reference Transformer improves significantly on longer contexts over its pretrain equivalent. However, Transformer performance on long-context tasks consistently trails the Extender, on both the easier NIAH-6 and the harder REST tasks. For the 920M models shown, the persistent attention memory footprint at 64k context is approximately 54.5 million features (109 MB at bf16) for the Extender, vs. 5.67 billion features (11.3 GB at bf16) for the (MHA) Reference Transformer, factor 104 reduction. sections.title: 5.3 Ablation Studies
sections.content: To better understand how each aspect of the Extender contributes to its performance, we run series of ablation studies. For these, we train matched 200 Extenders (𝑑model=1024, 𝐿=13, 𝑑 𝜖 =32) on ClimbMix for 4 tokens with shared WSD recipe, varying one architectural choice at time relative to the default Extender residual graph. Table 4 reports final validation loss, DCLM CORE (T-mono mean and overall CORE, centered) and RULER, for subset of the ablation tests performed. Attention Query Input In contrast to the Transformer, Extender has choice of what input to take for the attention query projection matrix: x, h, or some combination of the two, with or without RMSNorm applied to the input. The default setting is 𝑄 from RMSNorm(x) + RMSNorm(h). In the table, [𝑥; ℎ] denotes concatenation rather than addition of inputs. Many of the differences are marginal, however, two significant results stand out: 𝑄 from either ℎ or 𝑥 alone significantly underperforms on long-context tasks. Note that concatenated input, with 𝑊𝑞 that is twice as large, did not substantially improve accuracy.

sections.title: Input
sections.content: Residual configuration passes seen in Table 1, RMSNorm(aℓ + hℓ 1) as input to the FFN. Here, we test two ablations: eliminating as input, and applying an additional norm on h: RMSNorm(aℓ + RMSNorm(hℓ 1)). into FFN As the default From these ablations, it is clear that including in the FFN input lifts performance. However, compared to conventional Transformer, the loss from dropping is not catastrophic: much of the communication between layers is carried by rather than relying fully on h. For out-of-domain tasks, having in is much more important than having in the FFN input. The extra RMSNorm ablation reports mixed and likely insignificant results.

sections.title: 5.4 Limitations
sections.content: While the Extender with 𝑑 𝜖 = 32 scales well from 199M to 924M parameters, we have not yet been able to test it at much larger model sizes due to resource constraints. Similarly, our token budgets are largely limited to 20 the parameter count.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: In contrast with prior work on reducing the attention memory footprint, the Extender focuses on the persistent memory footprint: memory required between turns. The Extender separates the superposition channel focused on next-token prediction, from the concatenation channel dedicated to attention memory. For every size class we tested, 32 features of attention memory per layer was enough to match the Reference Transformer on short-context tasks, and outperform it on long-context tasks.

Knowledge distillation Hinton et al. (2015); Sanh et al. (2019); Gu et al. (2024) trains student using larger teacher model, often achieving higher token efficiency than training from scratch. To better understand differences in inductive bias Goyal & Bengio (2022); Battaglia et al. (2018) between Transformer and Extender models, we train three 198M class extenders: one from scratch, one with 924M Extender teacher, and one with 920M Transformer teacher. Here, all three 198M Extenders use 𝑑 𝜖 =64 and selects features from using the 𝑅𝑎𝑛𝑑𝑜𝑚 policy. All three are trained to 4 Billion ClimbMix tokens with 2k token sequence length. Both teachers were trained with 9B ClimbMix + 5B ProLong tokens - earlier models than the 18B reported in the main body of the paper. The Extender teacher is somewhat stronger than the Transformer teacher, on both CORE and RULER scores. Table 6 shows the results of this experiment. The two student models both consistently outperform the from-scratch model, showing that Extenders train well under distillation objective. The student led by an Extender teacher achieved CORE score 6 points lower than its teacher, while the Transformer teacher transferred slightly less knowledge, with the student scoring 6.7 points below 16 the teacher. On long-context RULER tasks, the two students achieved near-identical scores within the 2k training domain despite the Transformer teacher being weaker. These results indicate that under logit distillation, an Extender student learns approximately as well from an Extender teacher as from Transformer teacher.
